Title: Trace: a fault while the trace exception is processed is taken

Body:

`execute()` calls `execException(M68kException::TRACE)` without a try block, unlike the instruction handlers and the interrupt path a few lines below. On master, three kinds of exception escape from `execute()` this way:

- On the 68000 and 68010, an odd trace vector. With $4201 at $24, the `execute()` that takes the trace exception after a traced NOP throws an `AddressError`, and PC0 stays at $1002. No host bus error is involved, so any program that sets the T bit with a bad vector can cause this.
- On the 68000, an odd supervisor stack pointer. `execException()` throws `DoubleFault`, which leaves `execute()` and does not halt the CPU.
- On all five models, a `BusError` thrown by the host while the trace frame is stacked, the trace vector is read or the first word of the handler is fetched. The same happens with a supervisor stack that rejects every write: the CPU does not halt.

The change wraps the call like the interrupt path: `catch (const std::exception &exc) { processException(exc); }`. The bus or address error exception is then taken, and `processException()` halts if stacking that frame faults again, or on a `DoubleFault`. Moira already handles faults this way during interrupt processing, and while TRAP, CHK, an illegal instruction or a privilege violation is processed inside the instruction handlers. This change applies the same rule to the trace exception. It follows Moira's existing choice; the manuals do not settle the question for every model (see below).

On the 68000, the bus error frame now has the I/N bit set when the fault hits the trace frame, the vector or the handler fetch. I copied the `catch (BusError &e) { e.stackFrame.code |= 0x8; throw; }` that `execException()` already uses for an illegal instruction and a privilege violation. MC68000UM §6.3.9.1: "the processor is not processing an instruction if it is processing a group 0 or a group 1 exception"; §6.2.3: "The group 1 exceptions are trace and interrupt, privilege violations, and illegal instructions." Like those two cases, the bit is set for the handler's first fetch as well.

What the manuals say, per model:

- 68000/68010, MC68000UM §5.4.4 defines the double bus fault: "When a bus error exception occurs, the processor begins exception processing by stacking information on the supervisor stack. If another bus error occurs during exception processing (i.e., before execution of another instruction begins) the processor halts and asserts HALT. This is called a double bus fault." §6.3.9.1 gives the halt rule: "If a bus error occurs during the exception processing for a bus error, an address error, or a reset, the processor halts and all processing ceases." The same subsection also describes such a bus error being taken: "If a bus error occurs during the last step of exception processing, while either reading the exception vector or fetching the instruction, the value of the program counter is the address of the exception vector."
- 68020/68030, MC68030UM §7.5.4 (MC68020UM §5.5.4 is worded alike): "When a bus error or an address error occurs during the exception processing sequence for a previous bus error, a previous address error, or a reset exception, the bus or address error causes a double bus fault." MC68030UM §8.1.2 (MC68020UM §6.1.2): "If a bus error occurs during the exception processing for a bus error, address error, or reset, or while the processor is loading internal state information from the stack during the execution of an RTE instruction, a double bus fault occurs". MC68030UM §12 (p. 12-30), on the halted STATUS: "Once a bus error has occurred, any additional bus error exception occurring before the execution of the first instruction of the bus error handler routine constitutes a double bus fault." The contrary reading is in the processing-states chapter (MC68030UM §4, MC68020UM §2): "A catastrophic system failure occurs whenever the processor receives a bus error or generates an address error while in the exception processing state." The example that follows it, though, is a bus error within a bus error.
- 68040: here the manual leans toward halting. §7.6.3: "A double bus fault occurs when an access or address error occurs during the exception processing sequence—e.g., the processor attempts to stack several words containing information about the state of the machine while processing an access error exception." The general exception flowchart ([Figure 8-1](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68040UM.pdf#page=216)) sends a bus error after the vector number fetch, a bus error after "SAVE CONTENTS TO STACK FRAME", and a bus error or address error after "PREFETCH 4 LONG WORDS" to the double bus fault. Its note excepts only reset and interrupt ("These blocks vary for reset and interrupt exceptions"). The interrupt flowchart ([Figure 8-4](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68040UM.pdf#page=229)) also leads a bus error or address error on the prefetch to the double bus fault. §8.2.1 and §8.2.2 list access fault, address error and reset, but they do not say "only". So on the 68040, Moira's interrupt path already departs from the manual, and this change follows that choice.

If you prefer the 68040 to halt on any fault during exception processing, that would apply to the interrupt path as well, and the 68040 rows of the new tests would flip. I will adapt the PR either way.

Other emulators: UAE takes the bus error. Its trace exception runs inside the `TRY` of the execution loop, and the `CATCH` calls `bus_error()`, which halts only if `Exception(2)` itself throws. `exception_in_exception = -1` is set only on its 68000/68010 bus and address error paths. The MAME core in `Tests/ThirdParty` (68000 only) does not set `SSW_CRITICAL` in its trace microcode, so a bus error there is taken as well. Musashi halts only in `RUN_MODE_BERR_AERR_RESET_WSF`, i.e. while it writes a bus or address error frame. Both MAME and UAE stack I/N = 1 while the trace frame is written and the vector is read. For the handler's first fetch, MAME keeps N set, while UAE clears its flag before that fetch. This branch sets it, as MAME does and as Moira does for the illegal instruction.

Tests (all in `BusErrorTests.cpp`):
- "A bus error during trace exception processing is processed" faults the trace vector and then the first word of the trace handler on the 68000, 68010, 68020, 68030 and 68040. It checks that `execute()` does not throw, that the CPU is not halted, that PC0 is the bus error handler, and, on the 68000, bit 3 of the first frame word.
- "An odd trace vector causes an address error" (68000, 68010): no exception escapes, the CPU is not halted, and PC0 is the address error handler.
- "A trace exception with an odd stack pointer halts the 68000": no exception escapes, and the CPU is halted.
- "A bus error while the trace and the bus error frame are stacked halts the CPU" (five models): the supervisor stack is in a region that rejects every write, and the CPU halts.

On master these fail 38 of their 68 assertions. With only the try block (without the I/N line), the two 68000 I/N assertions fail. With the change, all pass. If the catch is narrowed to `BusError`, the odd-vector and odd-SSP tests fail.

What was run: the full ctest passes on this commit (26/26), including ExceptionMame, ExceptionUAE, ExceptionUAE020, the SequenceUAE and SequenceMame runs and the three SST runs.

Not covered:
- No hardware capture backs either reading for any model.
- What the 68020/68030/68040 stack in the bus error frame for this case is not described.
- On the 68000, the frame stacks the status register the trace exception has already switched to (S set, T clear) and, for a fault on the vector read or the handler fetch, the vector address as PC.
- On the 68010, the format $8 frame holds PC 0 and SSW 0, because an incomplete host `BusError` is not completed on the 68010. Master's interrupt path does the same.
- The address error frame of the odd-vector case is not checked. On the 68020 and later, an odd trace vector is unchanged: the 68020 core jumps to the odd address ($4201) without an address error.
- After the bus error handler's RTE, the pending trace is lost (it is not taken twice), and the partially or fully stacked trace frame stays on the stack, as on the interrupt path.
- A host exception of another type, thrown from a memory access function or a delegate during the trace exception, now arrives sliced to `std::exception` through `processException()`'s `throw exc;`, as on the other paths.
